title: New AI Conquers Stratego, a Game Where You Can't See the Enemy
summary:
Imagine a board game where every enemy piece is a mystery. You only learn its identity when you collide with it — and the lower-ranking piece is eliminated. That's Stratego, a two-player wargame often used to test how well AI can handle hidden information. Players arrange 40 pieces on their side of the board, then move them across to capture their opponent's flag.

Now, a new AI system has defeated top-ranked human Stratego players by a large margin — something no AI had ever achieved. Researchers from MIT, Carnegie Mellon University, New York University, and Stanford developed it using machine-learning advances. Their system, called Ataraxos, combines efficient training algorithms with new techniques for calculated decision-making when information is hidden.

Stratego is brutally hard for computers. The possible piece configurations number more than 10 to the 66th power — exponentially more than in chess. Past efforts, like Google's DeepMind, relied on computationally demanding operations that cost millions of dollars and still couldn't beat the best humans. "With Stratego, there is an explosion of possible universes you might have to deal with," says Gabriele Farina, an MIT assistant professor and senior author of the paper. "AI techniques that were developed for games like poker definitely could not scale in this setting."

To build Ataraxos, the team used self-play reinforcement learning: the model plays against itself many times to learn a strong "blueprint strategy." It achieved greater performance than the next best models while being far cheaper and less computationally demanding to train. It also outperformed top humans in other strategic games with different rules, showing it can be generalized.

The AI could someday help humans tackle real-world problems with hidden information, such as business negotiations or cybersecurity. "Having AI algorithms that are general purpose and can provably perform this challenging task so well is a big step forward," Farina says. The research appears today in Nature.
why_it_matters: Most AI headlines are about chatbots and images, but this result matters because real decisions — in business, medicine and security — are usually made with incomplete information, not on a board where everything is visible. If AI can handle that kind of uncertainty while being cheaper to train, it could reshape how negotiations and cyber defence are carried out, and it pushes the boundary of what machines can do without full knowledge.

background_read: In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue became the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov — but chess is a game of perfect information: both players can see every piece on the board. Stratego, poker and card games are different, because pieces or cards stay secret, and researchers call this 'imperfect' or 'hidden' information. It is much harder for machines.

Google's DeepMind (a London-based AI laboratory owned by Google, best known for building AlphaGo, which beat the world's top Go player in 2016) showed how much computing power these systems can swallow. Other teams, including researchers at Carnegie Mellon, built poker AIs that defeated professional players in the late 2010s, but those techniques did not transfer easily to a game like Stratego.

MIT, Carnegie Mellon, New York University and Stanford are major United States research universities, and their teams published this result in Nature (one of the world's oldest and most respected science journals), which means other scientists can check the work and build on it.

perspectives.description: The team achieved something no AI had managed before, and did it more cheaply than earlier attempts that cost millions. Because the system also performed well on other strategic games, supporters see it as a general tool that could eventually help with negotiations, cybersecurity and any problem where not all the facts are known.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — what beating humans in a wargame means
perspectives.description: Stratego is literally a battle simulation, and critics note that AI that plans well under hidden information can be used for military planning or online attacks as easily as for defence. Others question whether pouring research into games, however difficult, is the fastest route to solving genuinely useful problems.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a pattern in game-playing AI
perspectives.description: Historically, each leap in game AI has been about removing a barrier: Deep Blue proved brute-force search could beat chess champions, AlphaGo showed learning could master Go, and poker programs showed machines could bluff. Stratego sits at the next frontier, hidden information on a much larger scale, which is why researchers treat it as a benchmark rather than a hobby.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — from board game to real world
perspectives.description: The obvious next question is whether the same methods really transfer to messy real-world situations whose rules are not written down. That will require testing, safety work and careful choices about where such systems are allowed to act, especially when their decisions affect people who never agreed to play.
